newsitem.title: USA: Troubled generator cuts short Columbia's mission.
newsitem.headline: Troubled generator cuts short Columbia's mission.

text.p: Mission control on Sunday ordered shuttle Columbia to cut short its 16-day science mission and return to Earth because one of its three power generators was malfunctioning and could become unsafe.
Columbia, which blasted off on Friday, was to land at the Kennedy Space Centre on Tuesday afternoon at 2:34 p.m. EDT (1834 GMT).

It was only the third time NASA has ended a shuttle mission early. A fuel cell was to blame for cutting short NASA's second shuttle flight in November 1981 and a failed navigation device ended a 1991 mission prematurely.
NASA officials feared the troublesome power generator could spark a fire or explosion. The shuttle is equipped with three fuel cells and can land safely on two.
The fuel cell, which generates electricity by combining supercold liquid hydrogen and liquid oxygen, had degraded since launch.
"We're certainly disappointed," said shuttle commander Jim Halsell after he was told by mission control that the space journey would end early.

The Columbia's crew of seven were less than two days into a 16-day microgravity research mission. They were to light dozens of fires to study the behaviour of flame in zero gravity and grow protein crystals for medical research.
NASA's decision to cut short the mission came only a few hours after managers said the troublesome power generator appeared to have stabilised.
Rewiring the shuttle power systems and reducing the load on the malfunctioning fuel cell appeared to have slowed the degradation, mission control commentator Ed Campion said.
The performance of the fuel cell had been degrading since the shuttle was launched on Friday. It had briefly shown signs of trouble before blastoff, but NASA thought it was working properly.
The devices, which are located in the shuttle's fuselage, provide all of the shuttle's electrical power.
Columbia's crew of seven was to spend 16 days in space working in a laboratory mounted in the shuttle's cargo bay.
